```{r setup, include=FALSE}
source("R/setup.R")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=FALSE,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE)
r <- load_results()
source("R/refresh_figures.R")
refresh_presentation_figures(r)
m <- r$metrics[3,]
default <- r$metrics[2,]
f <- r$group_metrics[1,]
male <- r$group_metrics[2,]
fn_gap <- subset(r$gaps,metric=="FNR")
fn_interval <- c(-fn_gap$upper,-fn_gap$lower)
validation_dropouts <- sum(subset(r$split_counts,split=="Validation" & target=="Dropout")$n)
validation_found <- round(r$threshold_row$Sensitivity*validation_dropouts)
```

<img src="`r knitr::image_uri("img/dropout-lecture-hall.png")`" alt="Illustrative photograph of a student walking toward the exit of a lecture theatre" style="position:absolute;right:54px;top:34px;width:370px;height:462px;object-fit:cover;z-index:1">

<div class="cover-copy">
<div class="kicker">STRONG TIGER &nbsp; / &nbsp; INTRODUCTION TO DATA SCIENCE</div>
<h1>Student dropout<br><span class="gradient-word">warnings.</span></h1>
<div class="cover-subtitle">Who gets missed by<br>the same warning rule?</div>
</div>
<div class="cover-bottom"><div><div class="cover-team">University of Edinburgh</div>An enrolment model and its missed warnings</div><div>UCI 697 &nbsp; / &nbsp; ONE PORTUGUESE INSTITUTION<br>Analysis 05 NOV 2026 &nbsp; / &nbsp; Revision 11 NOV 2026</div></div>

???
Who gets missed when we apply one dropout warning rule to every student? To answer that, we need to know what counts as dropout, what we know at enrolment, and how a risk score becomes a warning. We start with the outcome that we can observe.
---
<div class="kicker">01 &nbsp; / &nbsp; DEFINE THE OUTCOME</div>

# What counts as<br>recorded dropout?

<img src="`r knitr::image_uri("img/campus-corridor.png")`" alt="Illustrative image of a quiet university corridor and classroom entrance" style="position:absolute;right:54px;top:195px;width:146px;height:238px;object-fit:cover">

<div class="evidence-grid" style="max-width:920px"><div><div class="hero-number">`r num(r$audit$rows)`</div><div class="hero-label">student records.<br><strong>1,421</strong> recorded dropouts.</div><div class="fine-rule"></div><div class="quote-line">A course or institution change also counts as <strong>Dropout</strong>.</div></div><div>

```{r outcomes, results='asis'}
slide_plot("figures/recorded-outcomes.png","315px","Counts of Graduate, Enrolled and Dropout records at the normal course endpoint")
```

</div></div>

.small[Target: recorded dropout by the normal course endpoint.<br>Graduate and Enrolled mean no recorded dropout then. Enrolled does not mean graduated.]

.source[Realinho et al. (2022), pp. 1-4. Enrolments 2008/09-2018/19; endpoint usually 3 years, 4 for Nursing. No causal or Edinburgh-wide claim.]

<div style="margin-top:10px;font-size:16px;color:#d8d2f0">When would we need to make the prediction?</div>

???
We used 4,424 records from one Portuguese institution. The outcome is recorded at the normal course endpoint, typically after three years. A change of course or institution can count as dropout. Graduate and Enrolled both mean no recorded dropout at that endpoint. With the outcome defined, what could we have known when students first enrolled?
---
# The prediction starts at enrolment

<img src="`r knitr::image_uri("img/enrolment-desk.png")`" alt="Illustrative image of a university enrolment desk" style="position:absolute;right:54px;top:182px;width:276px;height:311px;object-fit:cover">

<div style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr;gap:36px;margin:65px 0 55px;max-width:770px"><div style="border-top:2px solid #B5A2FF;padding-top:20px;min-width:0"><div style="font-size:15px;font-weight:650;letter-spacing:1px;color:#B5A2FF">AVAILABLE AT ENROLMENT</div><div style="font-size:39px;font-weight:650;color:#B5A2FF;margin:22px 0 12px">Age, grade and course</div><div style="font-size:22px;color:#F5F6FA">Inputs to the original model</div></div><div style="border-top:2px solid #55DFCA;padding-top:20px;min-width:0"><div style="font-size:15px;font-weight:650;letter-spacing:1px;color:#55DFCA">OBSERVED AT THE COURSE ENDPOINT</div><div style="font-size:39px;font-weight:650;color:#55DFCA;margin:22px 0 12px">Recorded outcome</div><div style="font-size:22px;color:#F5F6FA">Dropout, Enrolled or Graduate</div></div></div>

<div class="bridge-line">How much do the available inputs tell us?</div>

???
The prediction is made at enrolment, using age, admission grade and course. The recorded outcome is observed at the normal course endpoint. Later grades cannot be used to make an enrolment prediction, and financial fields with unclear timing were omitted. Now look at how the available inputs vary across outcome groups.
---
<div class="kicker">03 &nbsp; / &nbsp; LOOK BEFORE MODELLING</div>

# What do we know at enrolment?

```{r entry-plot, results='asis'}
slide_plot("figures/entry-profiles.png","360px","Training-set boxplots of enrolment age and admission grade by recorded outcome")
```

.takeaway[Higher median age in the recorded-dropout group.<br><strong>Admission grades overlap substantially.</strong> <strong>No individual outcome is determined.</strong>]

.source[Training only, n = `r num(r$configuration$training_n)`; associations, not causes.<br>Quiz 7 recommended Data to Viz; this prompted our figure review. [Boxplot advice](https://www.data-to-viz.com/caveat/boxplot.html).]

<div style="margin-top:10px;font-size:16px;color:#d8d2f0">How do we combine these overlapping signals into one risk score?</div>

???
These plots use training records. Students later recorded as dropouts were typically older, but the distributions overlap, including for admission grade. The counts under each box show the number of training records. Because single inputs only tell part of the story, the next slide shows how we combine age, admission grade and course into one risk score.

Figure review: Quiz 7 recommended Data to Viz. We wanted a compact comparison of the centres and spread. Its boxplot page reminded us that equal-width boxes hide group sizes, so we added the training count below each outcome. We retained boxplots for this comparison; they do not reveal the full distribution. Each panel has its own labelled units. This is our design choice, not an additional course requirement.
---
<div class="kicker">04 &nbsp; / &nbsp; BUILD THE WARNING RULE</div>

# From enrolment to a warning

<div class="capsule-row" style="align-items:center"><div class="capsule">Age, admission grade and course</div><span aria-hidden="true">→</span><div class="capsule">Estimated dropout risk</div><span aria-hidden="true">→</span><div class="capsule">Warn if risk reaches the threshold</div></div>

<div class="flow">
<div class="flow-card"><div class="step">01 / FIT</div><div class="flow-n">`r num(r$configuration$training_n)`</div><div class="flow-title">Training</div><div class="flow-purpose">Fit the model.</div></div>
<div class="flow-card"><div class="step">02 / CHOOSE</div><div class="flow-n violet">`r num(r$configuration$validation_n)`</div><div class="flow-title">Validation</div><div class="flow-purpose">Choose one warning threshold.</div></div>
<div class="flow-card"><div class="step">03 / EVALUATE</div><div class="flow-n accent">`r num(r$configuration$test_n)`</div><div class="flow-title">Test</div><div class="flow-purpose">Evaluate the frozen rule.</div></div>
</div>

.small[Course is categorical; age and grade are additive on the log-odds scale, without interactions.<br>Later and timing-uncertain inputs are excluded. Recorded gender is reserved for the audit.]

.learning-note[The regression lectures help us review these choices. Logistic regression required further learning.]

.source[Seed 20261105; approximately 60/20/20, stratified by original outcome and recorded gender. Model fitting and validation use no test outcomes.]

<div style="margin-top:10px;font-size:16px;color:#d8d2f0">What score should trigger a warning?</div>

???
The model combines age, admission grade and course to estimate a probability of recorded dropout. Once a threshold is set, a score at or above it produces a warning. We fit on 2,652 training records, chose the threshold on 883 validation records and evaluated the frozen rule on 889 test records. Recorded gender is used in the group audit. So what score should trigger a warning?

Original R formula for Q&A: `dropout ~ age10 + admission10 + course`.
---
<div class="kicker">05 &nbsp; / &nbsp; THE VALIDATION DECISION</div>

# What score triggers a warning?

<div class="split-plot"><div><div class="hero-number">`r num(r$threshold,2)`</div><div class="hero-label">One common threshold.<br><br>Highest specificity while identifying at least <strong>70%</strong> of validation dropouts.<br><br>Validation sensitivity:<br><strong>`r num(validation_found)` / `r num(validation_dropouts)` = `r pct(r$threshold_row$Sensitivity)`</strong></div></div><div>

```{r threshold-plot, results='asis'}
slide_plot("figures/validation-threshold.png","385px","Validation sensitivity, specificity and warning rate across common thresholds")
```

</div></div>

.source[Our illustrative target, not a university policy. Grid 0.05-0.80 in steps of 0.01; one threshold for both groups. We then froze the rule and evaluated its sensitivity, precision and errors on test records.]

<div style="margin-top:10px;font-size:16px;color:#d8d2f0">What changes if we warn at 0.31 instead of 0.50?</div>

???
On validation records, we chose the threshold with the highest specificity among thresholds that found at least 70 percent of recorded dropouts. At 0.31 it found 200 of 284. We then used that same threshold on the test data. The gold vertical line marks 0.31 and the dotted horizontal line marks the 70 percent sensitivity target. What changes when we lower the threshold from 0.50 to 0.31?

Figure review: We kept lines because the horizontal axis is a numerical threshold and the purpose is to compare how rates change. After checking Data to Viz's colour caveats, we gave all three curves different line patterns as well as colours. The curves remain descriptive validation rates, not confidence bands; the full 0-100% rate scale is retained.
---
# A lower threshold changes who gets warned

<img src="`r knitr::image_uri("img/support-review-files.png")`" alt="Illustrative image of a staff member sorting folders for follow-up" style="position:absolute;right:54px;top:182px;width:276px;height:311px;object-fit:cover">

<div style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr;gap:36px;margin:65px 0 55px;max-width:770px"><div style="border-top:2px solid #B5A2FF;padding-top:20px;min-width:0"><div style="font-size:15px;font-weight:650;letter-spacing:1px;color:#B5A2FF">MORE DROPOUT RECORDS FOUND</div><div style="font-size:96px;font-weight:650;color:#B5A2FF;margin:22px 0 12px">+`r num(m$TP-default$TP)`</div><div style="font-size:22px;color:#F5F6FA">`r num(m$TP)` at 0.31 versus `r num(default$TP)` at 0.50</div></div><div style="border-top:2px solid #55DFCA;padding-top:20px;min-width:0"><div style="font-size:15px;font-weight:650;letter-spacing:1px;color:#55DFCA">MORE FALSE WARNINGS</div><div style="font-size:96px;font-weight:650;color:#55DFCA;margin:22px 0 12px">+`r num(m$FP-default$FP)`</div><div style="font-size:22px;color:#F5F6FA">`r num(m$FP)` at 0.31 versus `r num(default$FP)` at 0.50</div></div></div>

<div class="bridge-line">What did the chosen 0.31 rule achieve overall?</div>

???
These are comparisons on the same 889 held-out records, using the same model. With 0.31 instead of 0.50, the rule flagged 107 additional records with a recorded dropout and 177 additional records without one. Both changes come from the threshold, because the risk scores stayed fixed. The next slide reports the overall performance of the rule chosen on validation data.
---
class: tradeoff detailed-metrics

<div class="kicker">07 &nbsp; / &nbsp; OVERALL TEST PERFORMANCE</div>

# How many dropouts did we miss?

<div class="metric-line">
<div><div class="metric-value accent">`r pct(m$Sensitivity)`</div><div class="metric-name">Sensitivity / recall</div><div class="metric-detail">`r num(m$TP)` / `r num(m$TP+m$FN)` dropout records found</div></div>
<div><div class="metric-value violet">`r pct(m$PPV)`</div><div class="metric-name">Precision / PPV</div><div class="metric-detail">`r num(m$TP)` / `r num(m$TP+m$FP)` warnings matched</div></div>
<div><div class="metric-value">`r pct(m$Accuracy)`</div><div class="metric-name">Accuracy</div><div class="metric-detail">`r num(m$TP+m$TN)` / `r num(m$n)` decisions matched</div></div>
</div>

```{r test-table, results='asis'}
mm <- r$metrics[1:3,]
tab <- data.frame(
  Rule=c("Always no warning","Threshold 0.50",paste0("Validation rule: ",num(r$threshold,2))),
  Sensitivity=pct(mm$Sensitivity),
  `Precision (PPV)`=ifelse(is.na(mm$PPV),"Not defined",pct(mm$PPV)),
  Accuracy=pct(mm$Accuracy),check.names=FALSE)
cat(knitr::kable(tab,format="html"))
```

<div class="bridge-line">The rule missed <strong>`r num(m$FN)` recorded dropouts</strong>. Who were they?</div>

.source[Test n = `r num(m$n)`; `r num(m$FP)` false warnings; `r num(m$TP+m$FP)` / `r num(m$n)` (`r pct(m$WarningRate)`) flagged. Sensitivity 95% conditional bootstrap interval: `r interval_pct(subset(r$overall_intervals,metric=="Sensitivity")$lower,subset(r$overall_intervals,metric=="Sensitivity")$upper)`. A false warning is relative to the recorded label.]

???
On 889 test records, the 0.31 rule found 187 of 285 recorded dropouts and produced 222 false warnings. The chosen rule still missed 98 recorded dropouts. How were those 98 misses distributed across recorded gender groups?
---
# The missed-dropout rate differs by recorded gender

<img src="`r knitr::image_uri("img/empty-tutoring-chair.png")`" alt="Illustrative image of an empty chair in a tutoring room" style="position:absolute;right:54px;top:182px;width:276px;height:311px;object-fit:cover">

<div style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr;gap:36px;margin:65px 0 55px;max-width:770px"><div style="border-top:2px solid #B5A2FF;padding-top:20px;min-width:0"><div style="font-size:15px;font-weight:650;letter-spacing:1px;color:#B5A2FF">RECORDED FEMALE</div><div style="font-size:96px;font-weight:650;color:#B5A2FF;margin:22px 0 12px">`r pct(f$FNR)`</div><div style="font-size:22px;color:#F5F6FA">`r num(f$FN)` of `r num(f$TP+f$FN)` recorded dropouts missed</div></div><div style="border-top:2px solid #55DFCA;padding-top:20px;min-width:0"><div style="font-size:15px;font-weight:650;letter-spacing:1px;color:#55DFCA">RECORDED MALE</div><div style="font-size:96px;font-weight:650;color:#55DFCA;margin:22px 0 12px">`r pct(male$FNR)`</div><div style="font-size:22px;color:#F5F6FA">`r num(male$FN)` of `r num(male$TP+male$FN)` recorded dropouts missed</div></div></div>

<div class="bridge-line">Female minus male: <strong>`r num(-100*fn_gap$estimate,1)` percentage points</strong> (95% interval: `r num(100*fn_interval[1],1)` to `r num(100*fn_interval[2],1)`).</div>

???
These groups account for all 98 missed records. To compare the rates, divide by the number of recorded dropouts within each gender group. We estimate a 20.3 percentage point gap, with a 95 percent bootstrap interval conditional on the fixed model and threshold. This describes the held-out data. The next slide checks whether the same pattern appears for false warnings.
---
# Who was more often warned without a recorded dropout?

.small[Among students with no recorded dropout in the test set]

<div class="comparison" style="gap:115px;margin:64px 0 45px">
<div><div class="big violet">`r pct(f$FPR)`</div><div class="label"><strong style="color:#b5a2ff">RECORDED FEMALE</strong><br>`r num(f$FP)` of `r num(f$FP+f$TN)` students flagged</div></div>
<div><div class="big accent">`r pct(male$FPR)`</div><div class="label"><strong>RECORDED MALE</strong><br>`r num(male$FP)` of `r num(male$FP+male$TN)` students flagged</div></div>
</div>

<div class="bridge-line">Do we see a similar trade-off when we group students by whether they left home to study?</div>

.source[Same 0.31 threshold and test set as the missed-dropout comparison.]

???
The previous slide showed that the rule missed a larger share of recorded dropouts in the female group. Now look at a different denominator: students with no recorded dropout. Of these, 138 of 431 in the recorded female group and 84 of 173 in the recorded male group were flagged. The same rule can miss students who later drop out and flag students who do not. Do we see a similar trade-off when we group students by whether they left home to study?
---
class: compact

# Do the error patterns extend beyond gender?

.small[Displaced = 1 means recorded as having left home to study. The dataset codes this as a yes/no field.]

```{r displaced-comparison, results='asis'}
source("R/displaced-audit.R", encoding = "UTF-8")
d <- displaced_audit()
tab <- data.frame(
  Threshold = sprintf("%.2f", d$threshold),
  Displaced = ifelse(d$group == 1, "Yes (1)", "No (0)"),
  `Missed dropout` = sprintf("%d/%d (%s)", d$missed, d$dropouts, pct(d$fnr)),
  `False warning` = sprintf("%d/%d (%s)", d$false_warnings, d$no_dropout, pct(d$fpr)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
cat(knitr::kable(tab, format = "html"))
```

.takeaway[At 0.31, students marked displaced had a <strong>`r num(100 * (d$fnr[2] - d$fnr[1]), 1)` percentage-point higher miss rate</strong> and a lower false-warning rate.]

.bridge-line[Across both groupings, these errors give us a reason to review warnings before offering support.]

???
After comparing recorded gender, we applied the same two thresholds to a second grouping, the dataset's Displaced field. At 0.31, the group marked displaced had more missed dropouts proportionally, but fewer false warnings proportionally. The same directions appeared at 0.50. Both groups missed more dropouts at the higher threshold. These are descriptive differences in model errors. Before anyone acts on a warning, the student's circumstances still need checking.
---
class: closing

<h1 style="font-size:49px;letter-spacing:-1.5px">Review the warning before offering support</h1>

<img src="`r knitr::image_uri("img/student-support-meeting.png")`" alt="Illustrative photograph of a student speaking with an academic adviser" style="position:absolute;right:54px;top:116px;width:330px;height:390px;object-fit:cover">

<div style="max-width:640px">
<div class="small">A missed warning can delay an offer of support. A false warning can prompt an unnecessary follow-up.</div>
<div style="display:grid;gap:14px;margin:20px 0"><div class="next-item" style="padding-top:10px">Check in with the student.<span>Confirm the record, ask what support they need and offer help.</span></div><div class="next-item" style="padding-top:10px">Keep support open.<span>Students who received no warning can still ask for help.</span></div><div class="next-item" style="padding-top:10px">Check capacity and validate on later cohorts.<span>In the test set, `r pct(m$WarningRate)` of students were flagged.</span></div></div>
<div class="small">This analysis did not test whether outreach prevents dropout.</div>
<div class="source">Historical records from one institution. The rule still needs evaluation on later cohorts.</div>
</div>

???
The two error patterns explain why this needs human review. A flagged student may benefit from a check-in even if they never receive a dropout label. An unflagged student should still be able to access support. Staff would confirm the records, ask about the student's needs and offer support where appropriate. We would also check capacity and validate on later cohorts. This study measured prediction errors. It did not measure whether outreach prevents dropout.
---
